nameStory: The 'cutleaf' part of this evening primrose's name comes from its distinctive deeply divided leaves that look like they've been cut with scissors or carved with intricate notches. Like other evening primroses, it gets the 'evening' part because its flowers typically open in the late afternoon or evening hours, often closing again by the next morning.
description: Cutleaf evening primrose is a low-growing annual wildflower that spreads along the ground rather than growing tall. Its most distinctive feature is its deeply lobed, almost feathery leaves that look quite different from other evening primroses. The plant produces small yellow flowers with four petals and grows in a sprawling mat, rarely getting more than a foot tall but spreading outward along the soil.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply cut, almost feathery leaves with narrow lobes that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch - completely different from the simple oval leaves of most evening primroses

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright yellow flowers with four heart-shaped petals that open in late afternoon, each about the size of a penny

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing and spreading along the ground in a mat-like pattern, never getting very tall but sprawling outward

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small capsules that split open to release tiny seeds, often with a slightly curved, club-like shape

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Reddish or purplish stems that feel somewhat sticky and have fine hairs, especially near the growing tips

habitat: In New England, cutleaf evening primrose is quite rare and typically found in disturbed sandy or gravelly soils, often along roadsides, in vacant lots, or in other areas where the ground has been disturbed. It prefers full sun and well-drained, often poor soils where other plants struggle to compete.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and develop their characteristic deeply-cut leaves, forming low rosettes close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time, with small yellow flowers opening in late afternoon and evening hours from mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue flowering into early fall, then set seed and die back as the first frost approaches.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain - this annual plant completes its life cycle in one growing season.

funFact: Despite being native to eastern North America, this little plant has become such a successful traveler that it's now considered a weed problem in places as far away as Hawaii, Australia, and Japan - all from a plant that's extremely rare in its New England homeland!
confusionNotes: The deeply cut, feathery leaves make this almost impossible to confuse with other evening primroses in New England, which all have simple, unlobed leaves. The low, sprawling growth habit also sets it apart from the tall, upright common evening primrose.
contextualKnowledge: With only 5 recorded observations in all of New England, cutleaf evening primrose is one of our rarest wildflowers - ironically, while it's spreading around the world as an invasive species, it's barely hanging on in its native northeastern range.
compareHints: Unlike the tall, upright common evening primrose with its simple oval leaves, cutleaf evening primrose stays low to the ground with deeply divided, almost fern-like foliage. While other evening primroses in our region can grow 3-6 feet tall, this species rarely exceeds 12 inches in height but spreads horizontally instead.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common evening-primrose is the tallest and most robust of New England's evening-primroses, with the largest flowers.
Small sundrops differs from its evening primrose relatives by staying low and sprawling rather than growing tall and upright like common evening primrose.
Among New England's evening primroses, northern evening primrose stands out for its smaller flower size compared to common evening primrose and Large-flowered evening-primrose.
Meadow evening primrose is much less common than its cousin common evening primrose, which grows much taller (3-6 feet) and has larger flowers that open in the evening.
Unlike the bold, large yellow flowers of common evening-primrose that can be 2 inches across, clockweed has tiny, delicate white or pink flowers only half an inch wide.
Unlike its yellow-flowered cousin common evening-primrose which grows tall and upright, pinkladies stays low and spreads horizontally.
Unlike its evening primrose cousins that typically have four-petaled yellow flowers opening at dusk, biennial beeblossom stands out with its pink flowers and incredibly tall, airy growth habit.
Large-flowered evening primrose stands out from other Oenothera species primarily due to its impressive flower size - much larger than common evening primrose or the various sundrops species.
Among the many evening primroses in New England, red-stalked evening primrose stands out primarily for its reddish stem coloration, while most relatives like common evening primrose have green stems.
Unlike the common evening primrose which typically grows 3-5 feet tall, tall evening primrose can reach 6 feet, making it the giant of the genus.
Bigfruit evening primrose stands out dramatically from its New England relatives like common evening primrose due to its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit rather than upright stems.
Yellow sundrops differ from common evening-primrose by blooming during the day rather than evening and having distinctive blue-green waxy leaves instead of plain green ones.
Among the evening-primroses in New England, Nodding Evening-Primrose is unique for its drooping flower buds - all other species have upright, erect buds.
